kit/session: players, entities, and replication scheduling

38 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Session roles and integrationConfigure callbacks before startingStart the session and process eventsThe replicated worldRoster, moderation, statsCommand hooksInterest management (area of interest)App messagesBackup hosting and resumeOwnership transferCoop lag compensation (session_rewound)Three tiers of entry into your codeLifecycle and replication pitfallsInternals and design notes

kit/session owns the live multiplayer session: stable player identities, roster, entity lifetime, replication scheduling, commands, pings, stats, moderation, interest management, and backup snapshots. It drives the lower-level kit/net registry and replication walks.

The package does not import Godot or own sockets. A game provides a transport send callback and forwards received packets and peer disconnects. Most Godot projects use kit/netgd or kit/boot for that integration.

Session roles and integration#

Player identity#

A client presents a random u64 reconnect token. The host maps that token to a Player_Id for the run. Reconnecting with the same token after the old connection has ended reclaims the player's ID, name, stats, and owned entities. Disconnected players remain in the roster so their seats can be reclaimed.

A token cannot take over a seat whose previous connection is still live. In that case, the new connection receives a new player ID; this matters when local test instances or browser tabs accidentally share the same persisted token.

Peer_Id identifies a current transport connection. Player_Id identifies the gameplay player across reconnects. They are distinct types and should not be stored interchangeably. Backup snapshots store token hashes, allowing a successor host to preserve reconnect identity without receiving the secrets.

Use kit/save to persist a token between application launches.

Events and callbacks#

Normal game reactions are queued and drained with session_poll. Synchronous callbacks are reserved for work the session cannot defer: creating an entity, locating it for interest management, serializing a backup blob, executing an authority hook, or decoding bytes whose reader is temporary. See Three tiers of entry for the complete contract.

Transport boundary#

Three connections keep the session transport-independent:

  • session_set_transport installs a callback that receives complete message bytes, destination peer, and channel.
  • session_handle_packet accepts a session payload routed from the transport.
  • session_peer_disconnected reports the end of a transport connection. A socket connection alone is not a player; the join handshake creates a seat.

Shared and authority-specific code#

Generated command wrappers, entity factories, and queued events provide common call sites on hosts and clients. Presentation code can normally react to the same spawn, state, and command events on every peer. Authority-specific work is still explicit in _then halves, authority steps, host lifecycle methods, and other places where only the authority can mutate shared gameplay state.

Entity factory and late join#

Boot normally provides generated, typed functions: <type>_spawn, boot_spawn_send/boot_spawn_cancel, and <type>_despawn. At the advanced session layer, session_spawn_make sends authority-side creation through the same Make_Entity_Proc used on clients. session_despawn similarly calls the installed free procedure on every role. A late joiner's welcome and complete world snapshot use the same reliable ordered channel, so entities are created before later deltas can refer to them.

Configure callbacks before starting#

Install these callbacks once in ready(), before starting the session. They remain installed when the session is reinitialized:

Odin
session_configure :: proc(s: ^Session, cfg: Session_Config)
session_set_transport :: proc(s: ^Session, user: rawptr, send: Send_Proc)
session_set_factory :: proc(s: ^Session, user: rawptr, make_entity: Make_Entity_Proc, free_entity: Free_Entity_Proc)
session_set_command_hook :: proc(s: ^Session, user: rawptr, hook: Command_Hook)
session_app_route :: proc(s: ^Session, tag: u8, user: rawptr, handler: App_Handler)

session_reset(s) ends the live run and frees its roster, registry, queues, profiles, and snapshots while retaining this pre-start wiring and configuration. The generated game-network detach uses it when returning to the menu so the game can attach again later. session_destroy(s) also releases the callbacks; use it when the session value will no longer be used.

Session_Config holds the session settings. Zero-valued fields select the defaults, so a zero-initialized config is valid. All durations are in seconds. The session converts them to tick counts, preserving timeout durations when tick_hz changes:

Odin
Session_Config :: struct {
	tick_hz:         int, // net ticks per second (0 = knet.DEFAULT_TICK_HZ, 20)
	interp_delay:    f64, // how far in the past remote entities render
	interp_adapt:    bool, // adapt interpolation delay (off by default; interp_delay is the floor)
	interp_delay_max: f64, // maximum adaptive delay in seconds (0 = the Kit default)
	command_timeout: f64, // prediction auto-revert horizon
	join_timeout:    f64, // client_start -> Ev_Join_Failed horizon
	backup_interval: f64, // backup-host snapshot refresh cadence
	max_players:     int, // cap for new seats (0 = DEFAULT_MAX_PLAYERS, 8); reconnects use their existing seat
	change_events:   bool, // emit Ev_Entity_Changed for each dirty entity per tick
	stream_budget:   int, // per-peer owner-stream bytes per tick (0 = unlimited; requires interest management)
	traffic:         Traffic_Config, // authority ingress: reliable, stream, and action token buckets
	fingerprint:     u64, // wire-contract hash override (0 = the generated default) — see below
}

max_players defaults to eight. Set it to a negative value only when an unbounded lobby is intentional; reconnects may reclaim an existing seat even when the room is otherwise full. change_events is off by default. Enable it when the game should repaint only entities touched by a state batch.

stream_budget limits owner-stream bytes sent to each peer per network tick. It requires interest management because per-peer routing is what makes individual budgets possible. Updates are prioritized by staleness, with distance as a tiebreaker.

traffic bounds what each seated client may send to the authority. Reliable and stream limits are per transport peer; actions is a narrower per-player budget shared by immediate co-op commands and tick-scheduled simulation verbs. Each Traffic_Limit has packets_per_second, bytes_per_second, and burst_seconds (zero burst means one second). A zero rate leaves that dimension unlimited; the named profiles install complete bounded values. This is separate from outbound stream_budget, which prioritizes what the authority sends to each observer and therefore requires interest management.

For a new game, use a named network configuration instead of filling this struct directly: kboot.network_profile(.Friends_Coop), .Listen_Server_Action, or .Dedicated_Competitive. The profiles materialize and validate Session_Config together with the matching ksim.Lane_Config, while still allowing ordinary field overrides. See Network profiles.

Schema compatibility checks are on by default. Descriptors are positional, so peers built with different schemas could interpret valid bytes as different fields. Before writing generated code, scriptgen recursively validates the types sent as raw bytes and emits NET_SCHEMA_CANONICAL: field paths, wire kinds and widths, enum storage, fixed bounds, input classes and constraints, message tags, and action access, prediction, argument limits, and scheduling. Platform-width integers, implicit-width enums, pointers, unsupported containers, unresolved nested types, and structs with hidden padding are build errors. Generated size/alignment assertions check that the target compiler's layout agrees with scriptgen's schema.

NET_ABI_FINGERPRINT hashes that readable schema. The complete generated NET_FINGERPRINT also covers entity ids, presentation events, RPC signatures, and the session's PROTOCOL_REV; the guard registers it as the session default at load. JOIN carries the fingerprint. Peers with matching fingerprints pass the compatibility check; a mismatch is refused as Ev_Join_Denied{.Version}. A checked host also refuses fingerprint-less clients from pre-check builds. Comments and formatting do not change the hash; changing a path, representation, bound, policy, or schedule does. Rebuild both peers after a schema change.

Leave Session_Config.fingerprint at 0 to use the generated value. Set it to a custom fingerprint when combining declarations from multiple modules, or to ksess.FINGERPRINT_NONE to disable compatibility checks for hand-built descriptors or tests. A session with no generated fingerprint is unchecked.

The generated hash cannot detect changes to a content table indexed by a wire value. It records that a Slot is {item: u16, count: u16}, but it does not record which item definition each ID selects. The same limitation applies to name-to-ID tag tables and other indices into game content. If a build reorders or renames entries, its fingerprint can still match even though a replicated item=1 selects a different definition on the receiving peer.

Use ksess.session_mix_fingerprint(base, contract) to include the table's canonical text in the fingerprint. Pass base = 0 to combine it with the generated default; assigning a content hash directly would replace the schema check. Peers then reject mismatched content tables during admission. kitems.items_contract(&table) produces canonical text for item registries, sorted so registration order does not matter. Cavecrawl includes its GEM/TORCH table this way.

In cavecrawl's ready, the game installs its entity factory, attaches the transport, and registers transport callbacks:

Odin
ksess.session_set_factory(&self.ses, self, cave_make_entity, cave_free_entity)
netgd.wire_attach(&self.wire, self.owner, &self.ses, MSG_SESSION)
netgd.wire_listen(&self.wire, "on_packet", "on_peer_left", "on_net_up", "on_net_down")

The allocator tiers#

Kit packages use three allocator conventions. The session stores an allocator and restores it at each entry point, as described in the second convention.

Explicit param: kit/net's *_make procs (writer_make, registry_make, …) take an allocator argument. The caller selects the allocator for each object.

Stored and rebound: kit/sim's Lane and this Session each store one allocator. Session.allocator is adopted from context.allocator at the first *_start and retained across reinitialization. The session restores it as context.allocator at entry points that allocate or free memory: the starts, resume, destroy, session_tick, the packet entry, session_present, the spawn/blob/owner/despawn mutators, and the subsystem writers (session_stat_column, session_profile_mine, session_set_successor_info). A roster name cloned in a packet handler and freed in run_destroy therefore uses the same allocator for both operations. So does a registry shadow allocated on spawn and freed on despawn. This remains true when the game's ambient allocator differs between calls, for example when it uses an arena or a tracking allocator. Set s.allocator before *_start to select a custom allocator. If it is zero, the session adopts the context.allocator in effect when it starts.

Ambient: comms, xfer, album, items, and the UI widgets allocate through context.allocator without storing it. A game using a custom allocator must keep context.allocator the same across each subsystem's initialization, use, and destruction. Free operations use the ambient allocator in effect at teardown.

An allocator-isolation test checks the stored-and-rebound allocator convention. tests/kitsession's the_session_never_spends_the_ambient_allocator runs a full lifecycle (start, join, both spawn paths, blobs, interest, stats, profiles, ticks, kick, leave, disconnect, a re-init, destroy) with a tracking allocator assigned to the session and a separate allocator monitoring ambient allocations. The test asserts zero ambient allocations. This detects entry points that fail to restore the session allocator, a mistake that may otherwise go unnoticed while the session runs.

Start the session and process events#

kit/boot manages this lifecycle: boot_host/boot_join start the session, and generated <game>_net_frame advances it and drains events through Boot. Use the lower-level API below when a game needs custom lifecycle ordering. These signatures show the main lifecycle arguments; the source definitions also include optional spectator and packet-channel settings.

Odin
session_host_start :: proc(s: ^Session, name: string, token: u64 = 0, dedicated := false)
session_client_start :: proc(s: ^Session, token: u64, name: string)
session_client_join :: proc(s: ^Session)     // transport is connected: ask for a seat
session_client_leave :: proc(s: ^Session)    // graceful goodbye
session_tick :: proc(s: ^Session, dt: f64, now: f64) -> (ticks: int, sampled: int)
session_poll :: proc(s: ^Session) -> (ev: Event, ok: bool)
session_handle_packet :: proc(s: ^Session, from_peer: Peer_Id, r: ^knet.Reader)
session_peer_disconnected :: proc(s: ^Session, peer: Peer_Id)

The host normally has a player identity, name, and stats. It creates its seat locally without sending JOIN over the transport.

Dedicated servers. session_host_start(…, dedicated = true) gives the authority a server seat flagged Player.dedicated. The welcome includes this flag in every client's roster. Games skip that seat when spawning avatars (if p.dedicated {continue}); the Kit lobby and scoreboard hide it, and session_count() excludes it. max_players therefore limits human players. Host migration is disabled for this role: a dedicated server must restart if it fails. Use this role when infrastructure runs the authority, through kboot.boot_serve in Boot. See examples/slopball/server_run.sh.

Clients call session_client_start when connecting begins and session_client_join once the transport handshake completes. If WELCOME does not arrive within join_timeout, the session emits Ev_Join_Failed so the game can report the failed join.

Call session_tick(s, delta, knet.now_s()) once per frame: it advances the net ticker (delta walk, streams, pings, stats, backup refresh, prediction expiry) and stream-samples remote entities. Then drain:

Odin
for {
	ev, ok := ksess.session_poll(&self.ses)
	if !ok {break}
	#partial switch e in ev {
	case ksess.Ev_Seated:    // this process now holds a player or server seat
	case ksess.Ev_Welcomed:  // (client) the host accepted us; the roster is seeded
	case ksess.Ev_Spawned:   // entity exists and spawn-time fields are available
	// ...
	}
}

session_set_born installs an optional authority-side hook for Ev_Spawned. With it, session_spawn and session_spawn_send deliver the authority's event synchronously after fields are set and announced. This lets presentation be initialized before a newly created node renders. Client spawn events remain queued so a welcome and its world snapshot retain their ordered batch behavior. kit/boot installs this hook through the generated entity table; low-level integrations may install it before starting the session.

Event halves and generated dispatch#

A kit/boot game can replace the manual event switch with generated event halves. Each declared proc pairs by name with a session event. The generated <game>_net_frame forwards them automatically and runs any declared cooperative authority step. The lower-level <game>_net_pump and <game>_events(self, events) remain available for custom frame ordering. Undeclared events are ignored.

Odin
@(gd_half)
cave_lobby_player_joined :: proc(self: ^CaveLobby, id: knet.Player_Id, rejoin: bool) {
	// every peer: repaint, log
}

// Authority consequence: announce and spawn for a late joiner.
@(gd_half)
cave_lobby_player_joined_then :: proc(self: ^CaveLobby, id: knet.Player_Id, rejoin: bool) { ... }

// _process
_ = cave_lobby_net_frame(self, delta, now_s())

The half names are the event names (_seated, _welcomed, _player_joined, _player_left, _host_left, _join_failed, _join_denied, _kicked, _backup_target, _succession, _backup_received, _owner_changed, _blob_changed, _stats_updated, _profile_changed, _state_applied, _command_executed, _command_confirmed, _command_rejected), except the entity cluster, which uses an entity_ prefix (_entity_spawned, _entity_resynced, _entity_despawned, _entity_changed) to distinguish it from the census hooks: <entity>_spawned runs before spawn fields apply, while <game>_entity_spawned and the typed <entity>_born hook run after the fields are available. Use _spawned for bookkeeping and _born for initial presentation. On the authority, kboot.boot_spawn_send dispatches the born event before returning. Each half's parameters correspond positionally to the event fields; invalid names or signatures are build errors.

An optional <game>_embodied(self, id) half runs when an entity type tagged avatar is born with the local player's ownership. It covers initial spawn, late join, and reconnect reclaim with one typed event.

Generated dispatch checks the role required by each event. An event delivered to every role (player_joined, player_left, entity_spawned, owner_changed, blob_changed) may declare a _then half for authority-only consequences. An event restricted to one role is dispatched only while the process has that role. For example, a host disconnect can produce two transport signals and queue Ev_Succession twice in one batch. After the first event changes is_host, generated dispatch skips the second client-only event. The succession half therefore needs no is_host check. Declaring _then for a client-only event such as Ev_Kicked, or a host-only event such as Ev_Backup_Target, is a build error.

The event union covers session lifecycle (Ev_Seated, Ev_Welcomed, Ev_Player_Joined with rejoin, Ev_Player_Left, Ev_Host_Left, Ev_Join_Failed, Ev_Join_Denied, Ev_Kicked), entity changes (Ev_Spawned, Ev_Resynced, Ev_Despawned, Ev_Owner_Changed, Ev_Blob_Changed, Ev_State_Applied, opt-in Ev_Entity_Changed), and updates to stats, profiles, and backups (Ev_Stats_Updated, Ev_Profile_Changed, Ev_Backup_Received).

Ev_Seated fires at session_host_start on the host and immediately before Ev_Welcomed on a client. A takeover retains the successor's existing seat and does not fire it again. Ev_Host_Left ends the run unless succession is armed; in that case, Ev_Succession also fires so the run can continue. Ev_Join_Denied distinguishes .Full, .Locked, .Banned, and .Version, allowing the game to explain the refusal to the player.

Ev_Resynced reports that a known entity received a complete field update, such as on interest re-entry or when a snapshot is applied over live state. Generated <field>_edge halves reset their stored comparison values without emitting edges. Games with custom edge detection can use this event to reset those values or present missed changes as new events.

Command events are Ev_Command_Executed on the host and Ev_Command_Confirmed / Ev_Command_Rejected on the client. They cover both immediate co-op and tick-scheduled actions:

  • confirmed: seq, entity, cmd, model;
  • rejected: those fields plus typed reason; and
  • executed: player, the addressed fields, reason, seq, and model.

The generated _command_confirmed, _command_rejected, and _command_executed halves receive those fields positionally. Reasons are Access, Rate, Malformed, Stale, Predicate, or Timeout; timeout callbacks retain the real sequence, entity, and command. model is .Immediate or .Scheduled, identifying the action model directly for games that use both.

The replicated world#

In a Boot game, use the generated typed helpers for gameplay: <type>_spawn, <type>_despawn, <type>_teleport, and boot_spawn_send/boot_spawn_cancel. They call the lower-level functions below, which are available for custom factories and batches containing multiple entity kinds.

Odin
session_spawn_make :: proc(s: ^Session, type: Entity_Type, owner := knet.PLAYER_ID_INVALID) -> (entity: rawptr, id: knet.Net_Id)
session_spawn_send :: proc(s: ^Session, id: knet.Net_Id)
session_spawn :: proc(s: ^Session, type: Entity_Type, entity: rawptr, set: ^knet.Command_Set, owner := knet.PLAYER_ID_INVALID) -> knet.Net_Id
session_despawn :: proc(s: ^Session, id: knet.Net_Id)
session_start_replicating :: proc(s: ^Session)
session_teleport :: proc(s: ^Session, id: knet.Net_Id)
session_owner_of :: proc(s: ^Session, id: knet.Net_Id) -> knet.Player_Id

Spawning has separate creation and announcement steps because the announcement carries a field snapshot. Create the entity, set its per-spawn fields, then send it. In a kit/boot game, each entity=Name:id tag generates a typed <entity>_spawn helper. It supplies the entity type and casts internally, so the caller needs neither a TYPE constant nor a rawptr cast. Use kboot.boot_spawn_send to announce the entity on the appropriate role. From cavecrawl:

Odin
sp, sid := spelunker_spawn(&self.boot, owner = p.id)
sp.x = SPAWN_X + f32(i) * 60
sp.y = SPAWN_Y
sp.hp = MAX_HP
kboot.boot_spawn_send(&self.boot, sid) // authority born hooks run before this returns

If validation or configuration fails before announcement, call kboot.boot_spawn_cancel(&boot, id). It removes only an unsent authority draft or a client-provisional predicted spawn; it cannot delete a committed entity. This gives complex factories explicit rollback without forcing ordinary Odin callers through a non-capturing callback API.

For a ticking entity, the helper calls boot_fire_spawn: the host creates the accepted entity and a client creates a predicted entity, as in sim.md's fired projectile example. The session_spawn_make/session_spawn_send pair remains public, and games that build entities directly can use session_spawn.

Call session_start_replicating on the host after setting up the world. It commits the registry's comparison copies and sends the full world to clients already seated. Subsequent network ticks broadcast deltas, and later joiners receive the world after their welcome. An entity owner calls session_teleport to mark a discontinuous position change on a streamed entity, such as a respawn or level change. Remote presentation then snaps to the new position instead of interpolating across the map.

The client-side factory:

Odin
Make_Entity_Proc :: proc(user: rawptr, type: Entity_Type, id: knet.Net_Id, owner: knet.Player_Id) -> (entity: rawptr, set: ^knet.Command_Set)
Free_Entity_Proc :: proc(user: rawptr, id: knet.Net_Id, entity: rawptr)

For most games, tag each exported entity scene with entity=Name:id and use the generated <game>_entities wrapper around kboot.boot_entities. It installs a factory that creates scenes under boot.world, records their nodes, dispatches typed *_spawned/*_freed census hooks, and dispatches born hooks for the host's own spawns when they are sent. Use session_set_factory for custom creation. Returning nil from make skips an entity. Each entity's wire record includes its length, allowing the receiver to skip unknown types.

Entity blobs#

Odin
session_set_blob :: proc(s: ^Session, id: knet.Net_Id, data: []u8)
session_blob :: proc(s: ^Session, id: knet.Net_Id) -> []u8

An entity blob holds one opaque, variable-length payload per entity. Use it for state that changes infrequently, following net.md's collection guidance: fixed arrays for bounded state, entities for live collections, and blobs for occasional variable-length updates. The game marks changes explicitly by setting the blob; the session does not diff, interpolate, or predict its contents.

The host sets the blob and sends it reliably to every peer. Ev_Blob_Changed fires on clients and the host. Full snapshots also include blobs, making them available to late joiners, backup hosts, and saves. Cavecrawl stores a per-floor inscription on the level entity this way; rejoining players read it through the same event handler as other players.

A blob is capped at 256 KiB and still has to fit the 1 MiB session packet that carries its update or world snapshot. Larger one-shot data belongs in kit/xfer, which chunks and paces it instead of blocking reliable state.

Use per-tick replicated fields for simulation state, app messages for transient events, and blobs for variable-length state that new observers need to receive. session_blob returns a view; copy it if you need to retain it. The session discards duplicate versions, including those received when a rejoin delivers the world again, so duplicates do not emit another change event.

Roster, moderation, stats#

Odin
session_player :: proc(s: ^Session, id: knet.Player_Id) -> (Player, bool)
session_roster :: proc(s: ^Session, allocator := context.temp_allocator) -> []Player
session_host :: proc(s: ^Session) -> knet.Player_Id
session_count :: proc(s: ^Session, connected_only := true, players_only := true) -> int
session_set_locked :: proc(s: ^Session, locked: bool)
session_kick :: proc(s: ^Session, player: knet.Player_Id, ban := false, reason := Disconnect_Reason.Kicked) -> (was: Peer_Id, ok: bool)
session_set_traffic_hook :: proc(s: ^Session, user: rawptr, hook: Traffic_Hook)
session_set_production_log_hook :: proc(s: ^Session, user: rawptr, hook: Production_Log_Hook)

By default, session_count counts connected players and excludes dedicated server seats. Player limits and checks, including min-players, ready checks, and max_players, use this count. Set connected_only = false to include departed roster entries, as reported by save/resume receipts. Set players_only = false to include a dedicated server seat in the count.

Call session_set_locked when a run should stop accepting new players. New joins receive .Locked, while players already in the roster may reconnect. session_kick delivers Ev_Kicked to explain the removal to the target. With ban, it also rejects future joins using that token with .Banned for the rest of the run. Bans are included in the backup snapshot and survive takeover. The game must persist them separately if they should apply to later runs.

Traffic refusals are observable without writing packet plumbing. The hook gets a typed Traffic_Violation containing player, transport peer, class (Reliable, Stream, or Action), attempted bytes, and that class's strike count. Return .Drop to report only, .Kick to revoke the seat, or .Ban to also deny its reconnect token for this run:

Odin
traffic_policy :: proc(user: rawptr, v: ksess.Traffic_Violation) -> ksess.Traffic_Response {
	log_traffic(v)
	return v.strikes >= 3 ? .Kick : .Drop
}

ksess.session_set_traffic_hook(&self.ses, self, traffic_policy)

With the generated/netgd transport, Kick and Ban also schedule the socket close after Ev_Kicked flushes. session_traffic_stats exposes admitted packets, bytes, and drops per player and class; session_traffic_dropped is the one-line netgraph total.

Disconnect events carry a fixed Disconnect_Reason: Graceful, Transport_Lost, Timeout, Kicked, Banned, Traffic_Policy, or Protocol (Unknown is the zero value). The reason crosses SES_BYE, SES_LEFT, and SES_KICKED, so Ev_Player_Left, Ev_Host_Left, Ev_Join_Failed, and Ev_Kicked report the same structured cause rather than forcing games to infer it from timing.

For production diagnostics, install session_set_production_log_hook. It receives Production_Log_Record, a fixed-size record of enums, player/peer ids, byte counts, ingress stage, and running count for malformed packets, rejected actions, traffic refusals, and disconnects. It contains no attacker-controlled text. Kit delivers at most PRODUCTION_LOG_EVENTS_PER_SECOND (16) per session second and increments session_production_log_dropped for the remainder, so a hostile peer cannot turn the logger into unbounded allocation or output work.

Odin
net_log :: proc(user: rawptr, record: ksess.Production_Log_Record) {
	metrics_count(record.kind, record.action_reason, record.disconnect)
}

ksess.session_set_production_log_hook(&self.ses, self, net_log)

Spectators. session_client_start(..., spectate = true) creates a receive-only seat. It receives world updates (spawns, deltas, streams, stats, chat), but the host rejects its commands, streams, and simulation inputs. Spectators bypass max_players, so they can watch a full room. session_count() excludes them, as do player checks and host migration. Player.spectator is available in every roster; the lobby marks these rows "(watching)" and the scoreboard skips them. Game spawn loops should check !p.spectator as well as excluding dedicated seats. To become a player, a spectator must leave and rejoin, subject to the normal admission checks.

Stats are named i64 counters on each player record. The host updates them and replicates a full stats snapshot to everyone at ~2 Hz when values have changed. They survive disconnects with the player identity. Column 0 is always "ping", updated by the session:

Odin
session_stat_column :: proc(s: ^Session, name: string) -> Stat_Col  // host; idempotent by name
session_stat_find :: proc(s: ^Session, name: string) -> (Stat_Col, bool)
session_stat_set :: proc(s: ^Session, player: knet.Player_Id, col: Stat_Col, value: i64)
session_stat_add :: proc(s: ^Session, player: knet.Player_Id, col: Stat_Col, delta: i64)
session_stat :: proc(s: ^Session, player: knet.Player_Id, col: Stat_Col) -> i64

session_stat_column registers columns on the host, typically in the Start handler. A Stat_Col stored by that handler remains zero on clients. Handles are 1-based, so zero is STAT_COL_INVALID; reads and writes assert on it with a message explaining how to resolve the column. On peers that did not register the column, look it up by name with session_stat_find. The lookup is cheap enough to perform on each read.

Typed player profiles#

Each player writes a profile row containing declared choices such as a character pick, loadout, ready status, or cosmetics. All seats use the same fixed-layout struct, and the host relays each row to other peers. Unlike stats, which the host accumulates, profile values are supplied by their players:

Odin
Pick :: struct { look, iron: u8, ready: bool }

// Tag the Session field. Script generation installs the profile at ready
// and includes Pick's recursive wire layout in the fingerprint. A changed
// layout rejects an incompatible join even when the type's size is unchanged.
ses: ksess.Session `gd:"profile=Pick"`

// Write and read the local profile row before or after joining.
// Before seating, the row remains pending. Seating assigns it to the player
// and starts replication without a second declaration.
ksess.session_profile_mine(&self.ses, Pick).look += 1

// anyone's row, in session_roster order (stable slots on every screen):
for p in ksess.session_roster(&self.ses) {
    pick, _ := ksess.session_profile_of(&self.ses, p.id, Pick)
    draw_row(p, pick)
}

The declaration installs the profile type through generated code. Each network tick, the session compares the local row with its previous value and sends changes. The host relays the table at the stats cadence and includes it after the welcome for late joiners. Every peer therefore has the table if it becomes host during takeover. Without scriptgen, install the type with ksess.session_profile_install(&ses, Pick) in ready, before *_start. Manual installation does not include the row's layout in the generated fingerprint check.

Ev_Profile_Changed{player} fires when a peer's view of another player's row changes; local writes do not emit it. The generated <game>_profile_changed(self, player) half receives those changes, and <game>_profile_changed_then handles their authority-only consequences. To populate the local row from saved game data, use <game>_seated(self, me), which runs on every role once per seat taken. _welcomed runs only on clients and would require separate host initialization.

For a ready-up flow, draw rows from session_roster and session_profile_of, require every row's ready before the host can Start, and use _profile_changed_then to spawn a newly ready player during a live run. The host must validate client-declared profiles. Authority-awarded values such as banked currency or inventory belong in replicated entity fields.

Command hooks#

A command proc may mutate only its target. Prediction, revert, and rejected command correction depend on that restriction. Put cross-entity changes in the verb's name-paired <verb>_then consequence. For example, taking loot uses a chest-only proc that returns the items taken. On the host, chest_take_then credits those items to the issuer's bag; that change reaches peers through an ordinary delta. If another player loses a race for the same loot, their chest command is rejected and its consequence does not credit their bag. The consequence's game parameter is the factory's user, the session's game pointer.

Use the untyped hooks for reactions shared across verbs, such as metrics, integration-test receipts, and replay logs. Route them by entity type to select the matching command descriptor. Generated command IDs are stable hashes of verb names, independent of declaration order.

Odin
ksess.session_set_type_hook(&self.ses, CHEST_TYPE, self, chest_hook)  // wins
ksess.session_set_command_hook(&self.ses, self, game_hook)            // catch-all for the rest

A routed type's hook receives exactly that type's commands. The host's own commands and clients' commands use the same dispatcher, which runs after the verb's _then. The installed hook survives session starts, like callbacks wired in ready().

Interest management (area of interest)#

Interest management limits per-tick deltas and owner-stream samples to entities near a player's focus position. It is off by default. Every peer still knows every entity: spawns, despawns, join snapshots, saves, and migration backups are unfiltered and include the complete registry.

Odin
// Install the authority's position callback before start or during play.
ksess.session_set_interest(&self.ses, 800, 120, self, my_locator)
my_locator :: proc(user: rawptr, id: knet.Net_Id, entity: rawptr) -> (x, y, z: f32, always: bool) {
	// Return the entity position (z = 0 for 2D). Set always = true for
	// shared entities such as the level or timers that should bypass distance filtering.
}
// Update each player's observer position on the authority every frame.
// The optional z coordinate defaults for a 2D game.
ksess.session_set_focus(&self.ses, pid, avatar.x, avatar.y)

The session applies filtering as follows:

  • Re-entry resync. The session does not retain filtered deltas for later delivery. When an entity enters a peer's interest, the host sends a full spawn tuple through the rejoin reconciliation path, updating its fields and blob together. This emits Ev_Resynced, since the entity already exists on that peer. Generated <field>_edge halves reset their comparison values without emitting edges. Custom seen_* values should also reset on this event; otherwise, earlier damage may appear as new hits on re-entry. hysteresis widens the exit boundary: entities enter at radius and leave at radius + hysteresis. This avoids repeated resyncs near the boundary.
  • Streams route via the host. Owners send their batches to the host instead of relying on an unfiltered transport relay. Packets already pass through the host, so this adds no network hop. The host forwards individual entities to each eligible recipient. Stream samples contain absolute state and do not need resync.
  • The game presents stale entities. An entity outside interest retains its last-known state on that peer. The game chooses whether to dim it, obscure it with fog, or leave it visible.
  • A peer without a focus receives everything. Filtering starts when the game supplies its focus position. Commands, stats, chat, and infrequent reliable messages remain unfiltered.
  • Filtering can change during a run. Joiners receive the host's filtering mode in their welcome. Later changes are announced to connected clients through SES_AOI. Client streams pass through the host's authority checks in either mode; AOI changes forwarding from whole batches to filtered per-recipient updates.

App messages#

SES_APP lets packages such as kit/comms send messages through the session's existing transport. Register a handler under a small tag, then write and flush its payload. The session checks the sender's seat before routing. On the host, from identifies the seated sender; packets from unseated peers are dropped. On a client, from is PLAYER_ID_INVALID, and handlers must check from_peer == HOST_PEER for messages that require authority.

Odin
session_app_begin :: proc(s: ^Session, tag: u8) -> ^knet.Writer
session_app_flush :: proc(s: ^Session, to_peer: Peer_Id, channel: Channel = .Reliable)
session_app_send :: proc(s: ^Session, to_peer: Peer_Id, tag: u8, bytes: []u8, channel: Channel = .Reliable)
session_app_send_to :: proc(s: ^Session, player: knet.Player_Id, tag: u8, bytes: []u8)

channel defaults to reliable. Use it for events or other messages that must arrive. Use .Stream only for tick-stamped payloads that supersede earlier ones, so a lost update can be replaced by the next send. kit/sim uses this channel for input and snapshot batches carried by SES_APP. Receivers route both channels identically, but dropped .Stream messages are not redelivered, and their ordering relative to reliable messages is undefined.

Host relay#

Several app-channel packages use a shared host relay. A client uploads a payload to the host, which attaches the sender identity resolved by the session and rebroadcasts it. Peers accept these identity-bearing messages only from the host and drop them from any other source. The relay's echo policy determines whether the author receives a copy.

Odin
Relay_Proc :: proc(user: rawptr, author: knet.Player_Id, r: ^knet.Reader)

relay_route    :: proc(hr: ^Host_Relay, s: ^Session, tag: u8, user: rawptr, deliver: Relay_Proc, echo := true)
relay_unroute  :: proc(hr: ^Host_Relay)
relay_begin    :: proc(hr: ^Host_Relay) -> ^knet.Writer                       // as ME, either role
relay_begin_as :: proc(hr: ^Host_Relay, author: knet.Player_Id) -> ^knet.Writer // HOST only
relay_flush    :: proc(hr: ^Host_Relay, to: Peer_Id = BROADCAST_PEER)

The envelope it owns, inside the SES_APP framing:

Code
[tag][RELAY_UP][payload]                     client -> host   (no author: it can't be trusted)
[tag][RELAY_CAST][author u64][payload]       host -> all/one  (the author the session resolved)

The calling package writes its payload through the same API on hosts and clients. The relay selects the upload or broadcast framing:

Odin
w := ksess.relay_begin(&c.relay)   // host: a stamped cast · client: an upload
knet.write_u8(w, CO_SAY)
knet.write_string(w, said)
ksess.relay_flush(&c.relay)        // host: broadcast (+ local echo) · client: to the host
  • echo controls local delivery to the author. When true, the host delivers its own broadcast locally, and clients deliver returned messages with author == me. kit/comms enables it so the author's chat follows host order. kit/xfer disables it because the sender already holds the transferred bytes.
  • relay_begin_as lets the host specify the author, for example when replaying chat history under the original speaker, sending a line with no speaker, or relaying an album payload under its publisher. Clients cannot submit an author through this API; author selection occurs only on the host.
  • An addressed cast never echoes. relay_flush(hr, peer) sends only to that peer. comms_catchup uses it to replay a log to a joiner without adding the entries to the host's log again.
  • deliver must queue work and return. It receives the payload and the resolved author. It must not write through the same relay while reading the payload, because that would reset the session's scratch writer and invalidate the bytes being read. Use the queued delivery described below.

Tags are one byte. relay_route asserts if another package already uses the tag and names the existing assignment: comms 0, combat's fires 1, xfer 2, kit/sim 3. Some packages use SES_APP without the relay. fire_announce broadcasts, while fire_announce_to sends a transient fire to one peer. kit/sim sends directly on the stream channel with its own tick semantics.

App message queues (appq)#

App_Handler and Relay_Proc run during packet dispatch. Each package queues decoded work in its handler so the game can drain it after packet processing. App_Queue provides the shared container:

Odin
App_Queue :: struct($T: typeid)

appq_push    :: proc(q: ^App_Queue($T), item: T)              // from the handler
appq_poll    :: proc(q: ^App_Queue($T)) -> (item: T, ok: bool) // from the game
appq_items   :: proc(q: ^App_Queue($T)) -> []T                 // what's still pending
appq_len     :: proc(q: ^App_Queue($T)) -> int
appq_destroy :: proc(q: ^App_Queue($T))

Packages expose their own public polling functions: comms_poll, xfer_poll, fire_poll, and album_poll delegate storage to App_Queue without changing their signatures. The container has no Session pointer, Session_Run entry, or run_destroy registration. Its dynamic array retains its creation allocator. The session and packages using ambient allocation can therefore share the container while retaining their respective allocator rules.

Backup hosting and resume#

The host periodically sends a complete recovery snapshot to the eldest connected client, which receives Ev_Backup_Received. It includes the identity table with hashed tokens, roster, allocation cursors, stats, and every entity as a spawn tuple. It also includes locked and the denied ban list, so a takeover preserves room locking and bans. Recovery resumes the last backup received. backup_interval controls the send cadence, not a maximum rollback window; network delay or loss can leave the available backup older than that interval. kit/save uses the same session_snapshot representation inside a versioned file envelope to save a run.

Odin
session_snapshot :: proc(s: ^Session, w: ^knet.Writer)
session_host_resume :: proc(s: ^Session, me: knet.Player_Id, name: string, backup: []u8) -> bool

The same session_snapshot bytes use two envelopes: [blob_len u32][game blob][snapshot] for a live backup, and kit/save's magic-and-FORMAT envelope on disk. A live backup is exchanged between peers whose compatibility was checked at admission: PROTOCOL_REV is included in the fingerprint. A save may be loaded by a later build without a join handshake, so the file carries its own version. See save.md's versioning rule for the statement and the third convention (the generated FNV field hash).

Call session_host_resume on a fresh session with the factory already installed. Other players are initially disconnected and can rejoin with their tokens to reclaim IDs, stats, and owned entities. The previous host can also reclaim its seat if it supplied a token to session_host_start; otherwise it returns as a new player. session_host_resume returns false on corrupt data.

Backups can also include game-owned campaign data, such as wave directors and AI clocks. As in kit/save's file envelope, these bytes are stored separately from the session snapshot:

Odin
Backup_Blob_Proc :: proc(user: rawptr, w: ^knet.Writer)
session_set_backup_blob :: proc(s: ^Session, user: rawptr, write: Backup_Blob_Proc)
session_backup_parts :: proc(s: ^Session, allocator := context.temp_allocator) -> (game_blob: []u8, snapshot: []u8, ok: bool)

Tag host-local fields gd:"backup" to generate version-hashed write/read procedures for POD, map[POD]POD, and [dynamic]POD data. See save. Install the generated writer through the callback above.

kboot.boot_migration coordinates host migration. The game declares four name-paired halves and installs them in ready; Kit schedules takeover, clears the old world, and limits reconnect attempts:

Odin
// Declare each callback with @(gd_half); unmatched callbacks fail generation.
@(gd_half) my_game_backup    :: proc(self: ^G, w: ^knet.Writer)  // host: the campaign blob (wire
                                                                 // the generated gd:"backup" writer in)
@(gd_half) my_game_took_over :: proc(self: ^G, r: ^knet.Reader)  // successor: read the backup and restore game state
@(gd_half) my_game_wiped     :: proc(self: ^G)                   // every peer: clear pools not managed as entities
@(gd_half) my_game_migrating :: proc(self: ^G, step: kboot.Migrate_Step, target: string, try: int)

// The generated my_game_net_attach installs my_game_succ_hooks.
// A custom shell may call this after boot_attach:
kboot.boot_migration(&self.boot, self, my_game_succ_hooks)

On Ev_Backup_Target, Kit computes and broadcasts the successor's connection address (netgd.Succession: addr:port on native, a reserved room code on web, allocated once per run). On Ev_Succession, Kit schedules migration at the end of the generated <snake>_events call, allowing ordinary event halves to finish against the old world. The successor then clears that world: the entity table's _freed hooks empty the per-type maps, and _wiped clears the remaining pools. It starts the announced transport, calls session_host_resume, and passes the game blob to _took_over.

Other clients reconnect within Kit's retry limits. A failed reconnect emits the succession event again to trigger another attempt; web connection requests are driven by boot_pump. _migrating reports each connection attempt and failure, including a missing successor or exhausted retries. The successor's .Taking_Over notification is deduplicated when kill -9 produces two disconnect signals. kboot.boot_take_over/boot_chase remain public for a manual Resume button, but refuse to run while the process has a live seat. Games managing their own transports, such as Steam, call kboot.boot_succ_config once to supply the transport configuration. Cavecrawl's acceptance-test act 4 kills the host with kill -9 and verifies that the run continues without manual intervention.

Custom transports can use the lower-level API:

Odin
Ev_Backup_Target :: struct { player: knet.Player_Id } // (host) holder changed — name them
session_set_successor_info :: proc(s: ^Session, info: []u8)
session_successor :: proc(s: ^Session) -> (knet.Player_Id, []u8)
Ev_Succession :: struct { successor: knet.Player_Id } // (client) host gone, successor named
session_backup_parts :: proc(...) -> (game_blob, snapshot: []u8, ok: bool) // copies

The session selects the successor player. It treats the connection info as opaque bytes, allowing a Steam lobby ID or an addr:port address. Live migration is supported only for the cooperative lane. boot_migration requires that no simulation lane is installed; this precondition is asserted in development builds. Simulation-lane recovery restarts the authority with fresh lane history rather than migrating live rollback state.

Ownership transfer#

An entity's network owner is the player allowed to send its owner-stream fields. Transfer that ownership with session_set_owner, usually from a command hook, to implement carrying, mounting, possession, or dragging a downed character:

Odin
session_set_owner :: proc(s: ^Session, id: knet.Net_Id, owner: knet.Player_Id)

PLAYER_ID_INVALID removes the stream owner. The entity retains its last streamed state while host-authoritative deltas continue. Every peer receives Ev_Owner_Changed{id, owner, prev}; a new carrier can begin attaching the entity's position to its own from that event. Transfer resets stream history and increments the warp marker, causing remote presentation to snap across the handoff. The old owner stops sending because registry_write_streams visits only locally owned entities. Its in-flight packets may arrive for about a round trip with the previous warp marker. The first sample with the new marker supersedes them without blending.

Coop lag compensation (session_rewound)#

A co-op shooter aims at the positions displayed on its screen. By the time a shot reaches the host, those positions are about a round trip plus the interpolation delay behind the host's live state. Testing hitscan against live positions can therefore miss a moving target that appeared under the crosshair. session_rewound temporarily restores streamed positions for the time the shooter saw:

Odin
// In the authority fire consequence, trace against the shooter's historical view.
ksess.session_rewound(&self.ses, by, &sweep, proc(user: rawptr) {
    sw := cast(^Sweep)user
    for id, m in sw.game.mobs { /* m.x, m.y READ where the shooter saw them */ }
})
// The live world is restored here; apply damage to the targets found.

During the query, every streamed body except the shooter's own is rewound. For other clients' bodies, the host uses inbound stream history. For its own streamed bodies, such as mobs or its avatar, it uses the outbound history retained by registry_write_streams with keep_history. Entities updated through host-authoritative deltas with no owner have no stream history and are tested at live positions. The host's own shots are also tested live.

The rewind duration is RTT + interp_delay: it includes both the stream's trip to the shooter and the shot's return trip. Using half the RTT would omit one transit; the derivation is documented in session_rewound's comment. session_rewind_secs(s, shooter) returns that duration for diagnostics or custom hit queries. Until the shooter's first pong arrives, only the interpolation delay is used, giving a shorter rewind.

Three tiers of entry into your code#

Kit's event-delivery conventions use poll unions for multiple event types and tuple-poll functions for a single event type. Callbacks run synchronously only when Kit needs a result or temporary operation state. The session applies these conventions in three tiers.

Choose the tier by checking these requirements in order:

  1. Use a pull callback when the session needs a pointer, position, or byte range before it can finish an operation.
  2. Use an atomic authority hook when game code needs state available only during that operation, such as a command's pending result, a packet's byte view, or the authority's current simulation tick.
  3. Use a presentation event for work that can be queued until the operation finishes without changing its meaning.

If next-frame delivery preserves the required information and behavior, queue the work.

Tier 1 — callbacks that return required data#

These callbacks return information the session needs before it can continue. Return a valid answer promptly, including for empty or unavailable input. Do not perform additional world mutations, sends, spawns, or despawns inside these callbacks; the session has not yet completed the calling operation.

callback asked why it can't be an event
Make_Entity_Proc on every spawn, both roles the registry needs the pointer before the spawn tuple's fields can apply
Free_Entity_Proc on every despawn, both roles the game must free the entity and node before the ID can be reused
Locator_Proc (interest) per entity, per tick, host the session cannot read your position fields
Backup_Blob_Proc (backups) per backup refresh, host the campaign bytes are the game's; the snapshot is written in one pass
kit/sim's Sample_Proc / Step_Proc / Resim_Proc per tick / per resim the lane cannot read or advance your simulation

Put game reactions in the event emitted by the operation. For example, Ev_Spawned follows entity creation on both clients and the host.

Tier 2 — hooks that use operation-local state#

These hooks run synchronously while operation-specific state is available. They may use ordinary world mutators, but must not re-enter the operation that called them.

hook fires inside the state that would be gone
<verb>_then consequences (net.md) the command's execution, host the verb's return value and the issuer, before anything else runs
Command_Hook / session_set_type_hook the same dispatch, after _then pre-result: the generic layer sees the verdict as it is decided
App_Handler / Relay_Proc (app messages) the packet switch ^knet.Reader views the receive buffer and is valid only during packet processing

An app handler must copy any bytes it needs after returning. Retaining a slice into the reader would leave it pointing at released transport memory next frame. Kit handlers decode the payload and queue the result for later delivery, as described in App_Queue.

Tier 3 — queued and scheduled presentation#

Presentation runs from session_tick or the game's pump after the state updates it depends on have completed. The game may drain an event queue or receive a scheduled callback:

  • Drained: session_poll's Event union and the generated event halves; the SES_APP packages' polls (comms_poll, xfer_poll, fire_poll, album_poll), which use App_Queue.
  • Kit-driven: generated @(gd_event) presentation, generated <field>_edge halves (fired by the presentation pass inside session_tick), and session_present's Later_Proc (drained on the same clock, interp-delayed).

Use tier 3 for new features unless they need a required callback result (tier 1) or operation-local state (tier 2). Document the specific requirement when adding a synchronous entry point.

Lifecycle and replication pitfalls#

  • Configure durations before *_start. Session_Config durations are in seconds. session_init converts them to tick counts at the configured rate. During a run, read the resolved fields (session_tick_hz(s), s.pending_max_age) rather than cfg.
  • Starting again clears the previous run. host_start / client_start / host_resume can reuse a session value. session_init tears down its registry, command context, roster, tokens, stats, and backup blob, while preserving the transport, factory, hooks, app routes, and configuration installed before start. Returning to the lobby and rehosting requires no rewiring.
  • Rejoins bypass locking and capacity checks. A known token may reclaim its seat even when session_set_locked is set or max_players is reached. To exclude that player for the run, kick with ban = true.
  • Custom transports must close kicked connections. session_kick returns the former transport peer so the game can drop it with netgd.wire_drop or an equivalent operation. Until then the socket remains open, though the session ignores packets from unseated peers. Boot's boot_kick performs both steps and schedules the close after Ev_Kicked is flushed.
  • Deltas contain sampled state (see kit/net's gotchas). A replicated byte set and reset within one network tick is not sent. Cavecrawl keeps level.won at 1 throughout the end screen so each peer can react to the field change locally.
  • The write guard counts violations in release builds. A client that writes a host-lane replicated field can diverge from authority state until the next authority delta replaces it (see kit/net's gotchas). Development builds assert with the class, field, and correction named. A -disable-assert build still checks fields, logs the first violation once, and increments session_guard_hits(s). A nonzero count indicates a local client write to authority-owned state. Expose it alongside session_malformed(s), the dropped-packet count shown by the netgraph.
  • Keep the factory's make limited to creation. Instantiate the entity and return it; put game reactions in Ev_Spawned. The host receives that event too, through session_spawn_make. Before adding another synchronous callback, check its required timing against the three tiers.
  • Use events delivered to the relevant role. The authority executes its commands directly and receives neither Ev_Welcomed nor Ev_Command_Confirmed. It does receive Ev_State_Applied, Ev_Spawned/Ev_Despawned, and Ev_Command_Executed, which presentation code can handle on the host. Use Ev_Seated or its _seated half to initialize per-seat metadata on every role. _welcomed would initialize only clients and require a separate call when the host starts.

Internals and design notes#

Trust and admission#

ENet is plaintext UDP: anyone on the path can read the wire. WebRTC and Steam provide encrypted transports and are the appropriate choices when traffic privacy matters. Client owner streams always route through the host authority gateway; it resolves the transport peer to a seated player, preflights the complete batch, verifies every row against current entity ownership and wire size, then relays it. Clients accept owner streams only from the host. stream_budget can limit outbound per-peer owner-stream bytes when interest management is enabled. Session_Config.traffic applies token-bucket rate and byte limits to every seated peer's reliable and stream ingress. The shared action bucket covers both command execution models. Immediate and tick-scheduled client actions enter one session_authority_action_admit pipeline after their model-specific header is decoded: authenticated playing seat, model-qualified dedup window, structural payload/target/descriptor, declared access, argument policy, tick plausibility, shared byte/rate budget, and bounded model queue. Authority_Ingress_Stats counts admissions and refusals by model, reason, and stage; execution callbacks remain model-specific after admission. Fingerprint checks detect incompatible builds. The write guard detects application mistakes in the local process. Neither establishes that a remote client is trustworthy.

The current defaults check decoding bounds, count parse failures through session_malformed, and commit reliable entity updates transactionally. Co-op and simulation commands use access checks and deduplication windows for exactly-once execution. The host checks owner-stream senders against entity ownership. Simulation inputs have structural checks and size limits; the game can declare a validator to check their meaning. Four separate admission points enforce receive-only spectator seats.

Named profiles bound traffic by rate and bytes, including structurally valid traffic from a malicious peer. Packet, field, message, profile, event, command, blob, and replication containers have semantic limits checked before allocation. Schema mismatches are rejected during join. These defenses cover malformed traffic, application mistakes, and version skew; they are not a complete adversarial-server policy.

For public lobbies or other play with untrusted clients, use an encrypted transport, tune profile budgets against measured legitimate peaks, and install the traffic hook for moderation and the bounded production-log hook for diagnostics. The state-hash probe helps investigate desynchronization. These controls limit admitted work. They do not provide account identity or DDoS protection before the transport, and the game must still validate the meaning of structurally valid player requests.

Gameplay patterns using session APIs#

The following patterns combine existing session APIs for common game features.

Character-portable saves let a character travel between servers while worlds remain with their hosts. Store the character's bag, appearance, and other portable data in a client-side blob using kit/save's file helpers. On Ev_Welcomed, send it to the host under an app tag (session_app_send(HOST_PEER, TAG_CHARACTER, blob)). The host validates and applies it to the avatar, and authority deltas distribute the result to peers. Save it on quit and at application-appropriate checkpoints. The host must validate all submitted values before applying them, including data loaded from a player's save.

Player-addressed state. Send private roles or objectives through session_app_send_to(player, tag, bytes), or through the typed @(gd_message) form (role_send_to(&ses, player, msg)) for POD payloads. Replicated fields are broadcast to recipients without per-player field filtering, so they cannot hold secrets from those recipients. Addressing does not provide end-to-end secrecy: the host sees the message, and ENet is plaintext. Use an encrypted transport and retain authoritative secret state on the host. Replicate only its public consequences.

Player-to-player trade. A trade must update both players' bags together, while a command may mutate only its target. Represent the pending transaction as a Trade entity spawned by the host when two players begin trading. Its replicated fields hold offer slots (item + count) and one confirmation value per side. Offers reference items; the bags remain unchanged until commit. Each edit is a single-target predicted command on the Trade. The host processes conflicting edits in arrival order, and a rejected edit reverts through command correction, as with a contested chest.

The excerpt shows transaction ordering. Before indexing either offer array, validate that the submitted slot is within its bounds. The authority must also validate item IDs, quantities, and bag contents before committing the trade.

Odin
Trade :: struct {
	owner:      gd.Node2d,
	net_id:     knet.Net_Id,
	a, b:       u64 `gd:"replicate"`, // the two Player_Ids at the table
	offer_a:    [4]kitems.Slot `gd:"replicate"`,
	offer_b:    [4]kitems.Slot `gd:"replicate"`,
	confirm_a:  bool `gd:"replicate"`,
	confirm_b:  bool `gd:"replicate"`,
	state:      u8 `gd:"replicate"`, // OPEN / DONE / FAILED; present changes through the field edge
}

// Declare by after the receiver so the framework supplies the issuer.
// The peer cannot submit a different player's ID as that argument. The
// predicates use it to restrict edits and confirmations to the matching side.
trade_seat :: proc(self: ^Trade, by: knet.Player_Id) -> (side: u8, seated: bool) {
	if u64(by) == self.a {return 0, true}
	if u64(by) == self.b {return 1, true}
	return 0, false
}

// Editing either offer clears both confirmations in the same target mutation.
// A later confirmation must accept the revised offers before commit.
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED)
trade_offer :: proc(self: ^Trade, by: knet.Player_Id, slot: u8, item: u16, count: u16) -> bool {
	if self.state != TRADE_OPEN {return false}
	side, seated := trade_seat(self, by)
	if !seated {return false}
	(side == 0 ? &self.offer_a[slot] : &self.offer_b[slot])^ = {kitems.Item_Id(item), count}
	self.confirm_a = false
	self.confirm_b = false
	return true
}

@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED)
trade_confirm :: proc(self: ^Trade, by: knet.Player_Id) -> (ok: bool, sealed: bool) {
	if self.state != TRADE_OPEN {return false, false}
	side, seated := trade_seat(self, by)
	if !seated {return false, false}
	if side == 0 {self.confirm_a = true} else {self.confirm_b = true}
	return true, self.confirm_a && self.confirm_b // the second confirm seals it
}

// Authority-only consequence. Recheck both inventories before moving the
// offered items; an item may have left a bag since the offer was made.
// Record success or failure in authority state for normal replication.
// Client prediction changes the trade table, not either inventory.
@(gd_half)
trade_confirm_then :: proc(game: ^MyGame, self: ^Trade, by: knet.Player_Id, sealed: bool) {
	if !sealed {return}
	if game_move_offers(game, self) { // validate both bags, then swap
		self.state = TRADE_DONE
	} else {
		self.state = TRADE_FAILED // present failure; no offered items moved
	}
}

Snapshots include the Trade's fields, so host migration can restore an open window and late joiners can see its current offers. The game must also handle Ev_Player_Left: the host despawns any table naming the departed player, so open offers do not outlive a participant's presence. A player may reclaim their seat later, but must begin a new trade after that cleanup.

Use escrow when an item must not be offered in two windows at once. The offer's _then moves it from the bag to the table on the host, and a failed commit returns it. Reference-based offers are sufficient when this exclusivity is unnecessary. In either design, predict changes to the trade window while the authority commits changes to the bags. The player sees the bag update after acceptance, avoiding inventory changes that must be undone when a prediction is rejected.

Owner-detected events. When a player's machine simulates movement, it should also detect events derived from that movement, such as a ball entering a cup or a cart reaching a checkpoint. The host's stream-sampled copy can be ~a fifth of a second behind the owner's screen. If the host alone detects the event, the ball may appear to pass the hole before the result arrives. The owner can report the result through either persistent state or a command:

  • State signature: the owner changes its owned fields to record the result, for example by stopping the ball inside the cup. That persistent state streams to the host, which checks its own predicate before applying consequences such as advancing the hole or crediting stats. Later samples still contain the result if an earlier sample is lost, while the owner's presentation already shows the ball at rest.
  • Command: when no persistent state identifies the event, or its consequence needs arguments, issue a predicted command. The target changes locally immediately; the host validates the command and runs its consequence hook after acceptance.

The game implements the predicates and state signatures. Use the command validation path for owner requests rather than adding a generic owner-event message without validation.

Adding a session subsystem (the touchpoint checklist)#

The session's subsystems, interest (interest.odin), profiles (profile.odin), stats (stats.odin), backup/succession (backup.odin), all integrate through the same ~8 touchpoints:

  1. Wire kind(s): claim the next SES_* id(s) in session.odin's table; netgd's netgraph name table follows it.
  2. Packet case(s): one case per kind in the packet switch. Role/seat gate first (rejections leave r.err clear because they are not malformed), then call <sub>_recv. A sticky r.err increments the malformed counter.
  3. A net_tick slot: if you send on a cadence, add one call in session_net_tick's sequence. Stats and profiles use the ~2 Hz lobby cadence; choose the appropriate cadence for the new subsystem.
  4. Late-join state: host_handle_join sends the world, stats, profiles, and current succession info. Include any persistent subsystem state that a late joiner needs.
  5. State scoping: put run state in Session_Run, which is cleared on each reinitialization, and pre-start wiring in Session_Wiring, which is retained. Add owned-container cleanup to run_destroy. State that must survive host_resume specifically needs a keep_* flag on session_init; profiles provide an example.
  6. Departure cleanup: remove per-player state through mark_left, where deduplication windows and interest pairs are also pruned.
  7. Event union, or the tier above it. New game-facing events join Event, and scriptgen's SESSION_EVENTS table if games should get generated halves. If your subsystem instead calls game code, determine which of the three tiers it belongs to before writing the proc type. For SES_APP messages, reuse the relay and the queue. Adding a variant fails to compile in kit/boot/forward.odin, which holds the kit's own forwarding table as one exhaustive (non-#partial) switch. Give the new variant a case for its Kit consequence, such as lane forwarding, a widget repaint, or succession handling. If it needs no Kit reaction, add an empty case with a comment explaining why.
  8. Fingerprint: if your wire shape depends on game declarations (profile rows do), include it in the build fingerprint so incompatible peers are rejected during admission.

See also: kit/net (the core underneath), kit/netgd (the transport binding), kit/sim (the server-authority simulation lane, which also uses this page's identity, replication, and moderation APIs), kit/comms, kit/combat, kit/items, kit/ui, kit/save, kit/steamgd.
